title: Graphs of quotient functions
log: 2026-11-01T14:46:40Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: No bank point teaches graphing rational and quotient functions with their asymptotes, stationary points and inflection points; the quotient rule card is only a differentiation skill that this point would use, and the power-function card covers only simple 1/x shapes at a lower depth.

draft.title: Graphs of quotient functions
card: To sketch a quotient function, first find its asymptotes and its intercepts. The graph may cross an oblique or horizontal asymptote, but it never meets a vertical one.
Stationary points are where f′(x) = 0. Check the sign of f′ on each side to decide if each is a local maximum or minimum.
A point of inflection is where f″(x) = 0 and f″ changes sign, so the graph changes concavity. If f″ is zero but does not change sign, there is no inflection.
Example: f(x) = x + 1/x. Then f′(x) = 1 − 1/x² = 0 gives x = ±1. Also f″(x) = 2/x³ is never zero, so there is no point of inflection.
draft.remember: Asymptotes first, then f′ = 0 for stationary points, then a sign change in f″ for inflections.

a.q: At which x-values does f(x) = x + 4/x have stationary points?
a.why: f′(x) = 1 − 4/x², which is zero when x² = 4, so x = 2 or x = −2. The value x = 0 is a vertical asymptote, where f′ is not defined, so it is not a stationary point.
a.clue: Differentiate, set f′(x) = 0, then solve for x.

b.q: For g(x) = 1/(x² + 1), g″(x) = (6x² − 2)/(x² + 1)³. How many points of inflection does the graph have?
b.why: g″ is zero when 6x² = 2, so x = 1/√3 or x = −1/√3. The numerator changes sign at each, and the denominator is always positive, so concavity changes at both. The point x = 0 is a stationary maximum, not an inflection.
b.clue: Solve g″(x) = 0, then check that the sign changes.

check.summary: No problems found. The card, both questions and the explanations are mathematically correct: f′ = 1 − 4/x² gives x = ±2, and g″ changes sign at x = ±1/√3, so there are two inflections.
